full_text_en:
Home Company v. Sendery Company — Contract Dispute

【Ruling Summary】

Unconscionability of a contract refers to a situation where one party to a contract takes advantage of its own superior position or the other party's lack of experience, among other circumstances, to set terms in the contract that are clearly favorable to itself, resulting in a serious imbalance of rights, obligations, and objective interests between the parties based on the contract, which obviously violates the principle of fairness.

Where certain terms in a contract signed by both parties appear to be clearly unfavorable to one party, but the establishment of such terms reflects the true intention of both parties, and their essence is precisely to balance the rights and obligations of the parties, a request by one party to rescind such contractual terms on the ground of unconscionability shall not be supported.

Plaintiff: Tianjin Development Zone Home Real Estate Marketing Co., Ltd., domiciled at: Tengfei Road, Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area.

Legal Representative: Zhang Meiyi, General Manager of the company.

Defendant: Tianjin Sendery Real Estate Operation Co., Ltd., domiciled at: Changqing Science, Industry and Trade Park, Jinnan District, Tianjin.

Legal Representative: Li Defu, Chairman of the company.

Plaintiff Tianjin Development Zone Home Real Estate Marketing Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Home Company) filed a lawsuit with the Jinnan District People's Court of Tianjin against Defendant Tianjin Sendery Real Estate Operation Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Sendery Company) regarding a dispute over a franchise contract.

Plaintiff Home Company alleged: On March 9, 2004, the Plaintiff and the Defendant Sendery Company signed a "Franchise Contract," which stipulated the rights and obligations of both parties, including non-competition and confidentiality clauses. After the contract began to be performed, the parties signed a "Contract Termination Agreement" on May 16, 2005, Article 5 of which provided: After the termination of the contract, Home Company must still comply with the non-competition and confidentiality clauses stipulated in the contract. However, according to relevant laws and judicial interpretations, these clauses are unconscionable. Therefore, the Plaintiff requested the court to rule to revoke the said clauses.

Defendant Sendery Company argued: The "Franchise Contract" and the "Contract Termination Agreement" signed between the Defendant and the Plaintiff Home Company were both agreements voluntarily reached by both parties on the basis of equal negotiation. The non-competition and confidentiality clauses stipulated therein do not violate laws, administrative regulations, or the principle of fairness. The Defendant requested that the Plaintiff's claims be dismissed.

The Jinnan District People's Court of Tianjin found the following facts upon trial:

On May 25, 2003, Defendant Sendery Company signed a "CENTURY 21 Regional Franchise Contract" with a non-party, Beijing Aifeite International Franchise Consulting Services Co., Ltd., whereby Sendery Company obtained the right to use and the exclusive sub-franchise right for the CENTURY 21 system within the Tianjin area and Langfang area (hereinafter referred to as the franchise territory) of China, and also had the right to further sub-franchise the use of the CENTURY 21 system to third parties. On March 9, 2004, Plaintiff Home Company and Sendery Company signed a "Franchise Contract," Article 7.3.4 of which, the non-competition clause, stipulated: "Without the prior written consent of Party A (Sendery Company), Party B (Home Company) and any related person or affiliated enterprise of Party B (as defined in the interpretation of this contract) shall not, directly or indirectly, as senior officer, director, shareholder, or in any other capacity or name, invest in, operate, or manage any other real estate intermediary institution or related enterprise (other than another CENTURY 21 franchisee) located within a 75-kilometer radius of the 'Approved Location' (or if exceeding the geographical scope of this franchise territory, subject to the scope of this franchise territory), or own or hold more than ten percent of the equity of such intermediary institution, during the term of this contract and within two years after its expiration or termination." Article 7.4.8, the confidentiality clause, stipulated: "Party B undertakes that the operational and business knowledge concerning the CENTURY 21 system, the CENTURY 21 franchise rights, and CENTURY 21 materials, as well as Party A's services and products, disclosed by Party A to Party B under this contract, including but not limited to information and materials disclosed at any time in meetings, seminars, training courses, discussions, regional business practice manuals, or other materials and/or single-store business practice manuals, are Party A's exclusive and confidential trade secrets. Party B agrees to maintain absolute confidentiality over all such materials during and after the term of this contract, and agrees not to use such materials in any other business or in any other manner without the specific authorization and approval of Party A." Article 14.13 stipulated: "Party B agrees that within two years after the expiration or early termination of this contract, it shall not establish any real estate intermediary institution or office within 75 kilometers of the Approved Location or any CENTURY 21 franchisee location, to operate the franchise business defined in this contract." On May 16, 2005, Home Company and Sendery Company reached an agreement on matters related to the termination of the "Franchise Contract" and signed a "Contract Termination Agreement," Article 4 of which required Home Company to return the originals of the "Franchise Contract" and its appendices, and Article 5 provided that after the termination of the "Franchise Contract," Home Company must still comply with the obligations set forth in the non-competition and confidentiality clauses of the "Franchise Contract."

The above facts are confirmed by the "Franchise Contract" and the "Contract Termination Agreement" signed between Plaintiff Home Company and Defendant Sendery Company, which are sufficient to establish them.

The Jinnan District People's Court of Tianjin held:

The "Franchise Contract" signed on March 9, 2004, and the "Contract Termination Agreement" signed on May 16, 2005, between Plaintiff Home Company and Defendant Sendery Company were both true expressions of the parties' intentions and did not violate national laws or regulations; they should be deemed lawful and valid. A contract lawfully formed becomes effective upon its formation. The parties are entitled to the right to voluntarily enter into and rescind contracts according to law. The agreements between Home Company and Sendery Company were voluntarily reached on the basis of equal negotiation. The non-competition and confidentiality clauses agreed upon by both parties do not obviously violate the principle of fairness. Therefore, Home Company's claim to revoke Article 5 of the "Contract Termination Agreement" signed on May 16, 2005, on the ground of unconscionability lacks factual and legal basis and is not supported.

Accordingly, the Jinnan District People's Court of Tianjin, pursuant to Article 4 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the General Principles of Civil Law), Articles 6, 8, 32, and 60 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Contract Law), Article 64, Paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Civil Procedure Law), and Articles 2, Paragraphs 1 and 2 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Proceedings (hereinafter referred to as the Evidence Rules), ruled:

Dismiss the Plaintiff Home Company's claims.

Home Company, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Tianjin No. 2 Intermediate People's Court, arguing: 1. The first-instance court's findings of fact were unclear. The first-instance court found that the "Contract Termination Agreement" signed between the parties on May 16, 2005, was a true expression of the parties' intentions and did not violate national laws or regulations, and should be deemed valid, which was incorrect. First, the contract between the parties was not based on a true expression of their intentions. The appellee Sendery Company used its advantageous position to sign the contract with Home Company. The first-instance court's finding that the non-competition clause agreed upon by the parties did not violate the principle of fairness was incorrect, because Home Company only operated a single business line—real estate intermediary services—and the non-competition clause in the contract was harsh on Home Company and clearly violated the principle of fairness. Second, the first-instance court's finding that the contract signed by the parties did not violate national laws or regulations was also incorrect, because the contract violated Article 5, Paragraph 3 of the "Measures for the Administration of Commercial Franchises," which provides that "franchisors engaging in commercial activities through franchising shall not cause market monopoly or hinder fair competition." 2. The first-instance court's application of the law was erroneous. The first-instance court's judgment based on Article 4 of the General Principles of Civil Law was incorrect. The non-competition clauses in the "Franchise Contract" and the "Contract Termination Agreement" signed by the parties precisely violate the principles of fairness and compensation for equal value stipulated in the above laws. According to Article 72 of the Supreme People's Court's Opinions on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Opinions on the General Principles of Civil Law), the non-competition clauses in the "Franchise Contract" and the "Contract Termination Agreement" signed by the parties are unconscionable. According to Article 59, Paragraph 2 of the General Principles of Civil Law, Article 73, Paragraph 1 of the Opinions on the General Principles of Civil Law, and Article 54, Paragraph 2 of the Contract Law, such clauses should be revoked. Home Company requested the second instance to set aside the original judgment and change the judgment to revoke Article 5 of the "Contract Termination Agreement" signed between Home Company and Sendery Company.

Appellee Sendery Company argued: The appellant Home Company's appeal requests lacked factual and legal basis. The first-instance judgment found the facts clearly and applied the law correctly. Sendery Company requested the second instance to uphold the judgment.

The Tianjin No. 2 Intermediate People's Court, upon trial, confirmed the facts found by the first-instance court.

The focus of the dispute in this second instance was: Whether the non-competition and confidentiality clauses set forth in the "Franchise Contract" and the "Contract Termination Agreement" signed between the appellant Home Company and the appellee Sendery Company were unconscionable to Home Company.

The Tianjin No. 2 Intermediate People's Court held:

The parties have the right to enter into contracts voluntarily according to law. The "Franchise Contract" signed between the appellant Home Company and the appellee Sendery Company was voluntarily concluded by both parties. The non-competition and confidentiality clauses set forth in the contract were intended to prevent Home Company, as a franchisee, from using the business secrets of Sendery Company that it had obtained to engage in unfair competition with Sendery Company, thereby protecting Sendery Company's legitimate interests. These clauses do not violate national laws or administrative regulations, and because they are for a certain period, they do not necessarily lead to market monopoly or hinder fair competition. Although the contract was a standard form provided by Sendery Company, the relevant terms in the contract, such as the meanings of "related person" and "affiliated enterprise" in the non-competition clause, were clearly defined in the contract. At the time of entering into the contract, Home Company was aware of this content but did not raise any objection and actually accepted and signed the contract text. Therefore, the "Franchise Contract" was the result of the parties' autonomy of will, and once formed, the contract produced legal binding force on both parties. Subsequently, Home Company terminated the "Franchise Contract" with Sendery Company for certain reasons, and on the basis of mutual agreement, they jointly entered into the "Contract Termination Agreement." In this agreement, Home Company again made a commitment to "comply with the non-competition obligations and confidentiality clauses stipulated in the contract," which should be strictly performed in accordance with the agreement.

Regarding whether the non-competition and confidentiality clauses in the "Franchise Contract" and the "Contract Termination Agreement" in this case were unconscionable, according to Article 72 of the Opinions on the General Principles of Civil Law, which provides that "a contract may be deemed unconscionable if one party takes advantage of its superior position or the other party's lack of experience, resulting in a situation where the rights and obligations of the parties obviously violate the principles of fairness and compensation for equal value," the determination of unconscionability can be examined from the following two aspects:

First, examine whether the contract is obviously unfair to one party. According to the relevant provisions of the General Principles of Civil Law and the Contract Law, entering into a contract, as a civil juristic act of both parties, should implement the principle of fairness. The essence of the fairness principle is to balance the interests of the parties to the contract. Therefore, the determination of unconscionability of a contract should be comprehensively measured by whether the rights and obligations of the parties are reciprocal, whether the benefits obtained by one party or the losses suffered by the other party violate the law or trade practices, among other factors. In this case, the appellant Home Company, by signing the contract with the appellee Sendery Company, enjoyed the right to franchise operations and consequently obtained Sendery Company's business secrets; therefore, it should abide by the non-competition and confidentiality obligations stipulated in the contract. The rights and obligations of the parties are essentially reciprocal. The contract signed by the parties involves the real estate intermediary industry, which heavily relies on information and data. Therefore, based on voluntariness, setting non-competition and confidentiality clauses when entering into the "Franchise Contract" was intended to prevent Home Company, as a franchisee, from using the business secrets of Sendery Company it had obtained to engage in unfair competition with Sendery Company, thereby protecting Sendery Company's legitimate interests. On the surface, these clauses seem to tilt the balance in favor of Sendery Company's interests, but in fact, once the "Franchise Contract" was formed and performed, Home Company could lawfully obtain part of Sendery Company's business secrets, a result that is irreversible. Even if the contract is rescinded, terminated, or expires, Home Company would still retain this part of the business secrets. Sendery Company could only prevent or control Home Company's unfair competition by establishing seemingly unequal non-competition and confidentiality clauses in the contract. Therefore, in this case, the establishment of the non-competition and confidentiality clauses was in fact fair to both parties, consistent with the trade practices of the specific industry of real estate intermediation, and did not violate national laws or administrative regulations. Moreover, because they are for a certain period, they do not necessarily lead to market monopoly or hinder fair competition.

Second, examine whether one party intentionally took advantage of its superior position or the other party's carelessness or lack of experience in entering into the contract. The so-called taking advantage of a superior position refers to a party using its economic or other advantages to make it difficult for the other party to refuse contract terms that are obviously unfavorable to it; the so-called lack of experience refers to a lack of general life experience or transaction experience. In an unconscionable contract, the party whose interests are harmed often accepts the contract terms proposed by the other party due to lack of experience, or lack of the ability to correctly understand the relevant content of the contract, or due to some urgent circumstance, rather than out of genuine voluntariness. In this case, although the appellee Sendery Company appeared to have a certain advantage at the time of signing, the appellant Home Company was not in an urgent situation when signing the contract, and as a company specializing in real estate intermediary services, it did not have a problem of lacking industry experience. Although the contract was a standard form provided by Sendery Company, the relevant terms in the contract, including the meanings of "related person" and "affiliated enterprise" in the non-competition clause, were clearly defined in the contract. At the time of entering into the contract, Home Company was aware of this content and did not raise any objection. Therefore, the formation of the "Franchise Contract" reflected the principle of autonomy of will of the parties. Once formed, the contract should produce legal binding force on both parties. Subsequently, on the basis of mutual agreement, the parties jointly entered into the "Contract Termination Agreement." In this agreement, Home Company again made a commitment to "comply with the non-competition obligations and confidentiality clauses stipulated in the contract," which should also be strictly performed in accordance with the agreement. It is particularly important to note that although Sendery Company appeared to have a certain advantage at the time of signing, with the formation and performance of the contract, especially Home Company's actual possession of Sendery Company's business secrets, Sendery Company's so-called advantageous position no longer existed, and the parties were actually in an equal position.

Furthermore, regarding the confidentiality obligations stipulated in Article 5 of the "Contract Termination Agreement," as they fall within the scope of ancillary obligations of the contract, they neither constitute unconscionability nor violate the provisions of the Contract Law.

Accordingly, the Tianjin No. 2 Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Article 153, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law, ruled:

Appeal dismissed, and the original judgment affirmed.
